lessons.title: कैसे (kaise) — "how," another of the k- questions

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: You already met क्या (kyā, "what"). Here is its sibling — and, like all of Hindi's question-words, it starts with k-.
(Skim if you read Devanagari.) क (ka) + ै (the ai-mātrā) becomes कै (kai); स (sa) + े (the e-mātrā) becomes से (se). Read कै, से becomes kaise.

कैसे (kaise, "how") from Sanskrit कीदृश (kīdṛśa, "of what kind") / the interrogative stem क- (ka-), from Proto-Indo-European kʷo- — the same question-root behind English wh- (what, who, how) and Latin qu-. Notice the pattern: Hindi's question-words are nearly all k- words — kyā (what), kaun (who), kab (when), kahāṁ (where), kaise (how). Learn to hear the k- and you can spot a question.

The adjective form कैसा (kaisā) changes to match what it describes: kaisā (m.), kaisī (f.), kaise (m. plural / respectful). Because the respectful "you" (āp) takes a plural verb, "how are you?" uses the plural कैसे — that is the form you will use next.
क (ka) + ै (the ai-mātrā) becomes कै (kai); स (sa) + े (the e-mātrā) becomes से (se). Read कै, से becomes kaise.

lessons.title: आप कैसे हैं? (āp kaise haiṁ?) — "how are you?"

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Three words you already own, assembled into the first thing you ask after hello.
हैं is है (hai, "is") + the anusvāra dot ं becomes हैं (haiṁ), the nasalised plural. Everything else — आप (āp), कैसे (kaise) — you have met.

आप कैसे हैं? = आप (āp, respectful "you") + कैसे (kaise, "how") + हैं (haiṁ, "are") — literally "you how are?" Hindi keeps the verb last, exactly as in Chapter 2's merā nām … hai. And because āp is grammatically plural (that is how Hindi shows respect), its verb is the plural haiṁ, not the singular hai.

To an elder or a stranger: आप कैसे हैं? To a friend (tum): तुम कैसे हो? (tum kaise ho? — ho is the familiar "are"). To no one in particular you would never drop to tū. Match the "you" to the verb: āp … haiṁ, tum … ho.

lessons.title: मैं (maiṁ) — "I," the m- of the first person

segments.text: To answer "how are you?" you first need "I." In Chapter 2 you learned merā ("my"); here is its owner.
म (ma) + ै (the ai-mātrā) + the anusvāra nasal ं becomes मैं (maiṁ). One nasal syllable.

मैं (maiṁ, "I") from Sanskrit मया (mayā, "by me"), on the first-person root म- (ma-) — the same root that gave you merā ("my") last chapter, and the same m- behind English me, my, mine and Latin mē. Hindi's "I," its "my," and English's "me/my" all grow from one ancient first-person sound.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the pronoun you can often drop

segments.text: Hindi verbs carry the person in their ending, so maiṁ is frequently left out once context is clear — much like Spanish or Latin. You will still learn it first, because the answer to āp kaise haiṁ? begins with it: maiṁ …
म (ma) + ै (ai) + the anusvāra ं becomes मैं (maiṁ) (maiṃ). One nasal syllable.

segments.text: Chapter 2 gave you hai ("is"). This is the same verb in the first person — "I am."
ह (ha) + ू (the long-u mātrā) becomes हू (hū); the chandrabindu ँ nasalises it becomes हूँ (hūṁ).

हूँ (hūṁ, "am") from Sanskrit अस्मि (asmi, "I am") — the first-person of the very root that gave you hai. That root, PIE h₁es-, is the "to be" of the whole family: Sanskrit asmi becomes English am, Latin sum, Greek eimi; Sanskrit asti becomes hai / English is. So the Hindi copula lines up with English person by person: हूँ am, है is, हैं are.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the "to be" table so far

utterances: person: I. Hindi: maiṁ hūṁ. English: I am.
person: you (resp.) Hindi: āp haiṁ. English: you are.
person: he/she/it. Hindi: vah hai. English: he/she is.

segments.text: The verb होना (honā, "to be") is the frame every sentence hangs on; you now have three of its faces.

lessons.title: ठीक (ṭhīk) — "fine," and how to answer
lessons.gloss: fine, well, correct — and the reply "मैं ठीक हूँ"

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: The word that answers "how are you?" — and does a dozen other jobs besides.
ठ (ṭha, a retroflex th — tongue curled back to the roof of the mouth).
ी (the long-ī mātrā) + क (ka) becomes ठीक (ṭhīk). The retroflex ट-ठ-ड series is a hallmark of Indian languages; the tongue touches further back than for an English "t."

ठीक (ṭhīk) means "correct, right, fine, exactly, OK." It is a genuinely native Indian word — no European cousin to hand — and one of the most useful in the language: ṭhīk hai ("OK / agreed"), ṭhīk samay ("the right time"), sab ṭhīk? ("all well?"). Not every word has a far-flung cognate, and that is worth seeing too: ṭhīk is Indian to the core.
Put it together with Chapter 3's atoms: मैं ठीक हूँ (maiṁ ṭhīk hūṁ) — "I am fine." Literally "I fine am," verb last. Add thanks: maiṁ ṭhīk hūṁ, dhanyavād. And the whole exchange stands:
— āp kaise haiṁ? ("How are you?") — maiṁ ṭhīk hūṁ, dhanyavād. ("I'm fine, thank you.")
ठ (ṭha, a retroflex th — tongue curled to the roof of the mouth) + ी (long =i) + क (ka) becomes ठीक. The retroflex ट-ठ-ड series is a hallmark of Indian sound.

lessons.title: आपका स्वागत है (āpkā svāgat hai) — "you're welcome"

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page

segments.text: When someone thanks you, this is what you say back — and it hides a word Sanskrit uses whole, unchanged.
The key word is स्वागत (svāgat): the conjunct स्व (स् s + व va becomes sva) + ग (ga) + त (ta). Add आपका (āpkā, "your," from Chapter 2) and है (hai, "is").

आपका स्वागत है = "your welcome is" becomes "you are welcome." The heart of it, स्वागत (svāgat, "welcome"), is Sanskrit सु (su-, "well, good") + आगत (āgata, "come") — literally "well come," exactly like English welcome. Two deep roots hide inside:
su- "good" is the twin of Greek eu- (euphoria, eulogy).
āgata is from the root गम् (gam, "to go/come"), cousin of English come.
Sanskrit's own svāgatam is this very word, unchanged — here it is again, worn into everyday Hindi.
The key word स्वागत (svāgat): the conjunct स्व (स् s.
व va becomes sva) + ग (ga) + त (ta), with आपका (āpkā, “your”) and है (hai).

blocks.title: What you've built — roots you now carry

segments.text: kaise from the interrogative k- (PIE kʷo-), cousin of English how/what.
maiṁ from ma- (PIE me-), cousin of English me/my.
hūṁ from Sanskrit asmi, cousin of English am.
svāgat from su + āgata = "well come," matching English welcome.
A stranger asks āp kaise haiṁ? — give a complete, polite reply, then thank-and-welcome the exchange back. (Maiṁ ṭhīk hūṁ, dhanyavād. — and if thanked, āpkā svāgat hai.)
